title_en: Xu Liang v. Shanghai Culture and Art Newspaper and Zhao Weichang — dispute over infringement of reputation rights

full_text_en:
Xu Liang v. Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette, Zhao Weichang — dispute over infringement of reputation rights

Plaintiff: Xu Liang, male, 29 years old, an active-duty soldier of a certain unit of the People's Liberation Army.

Agent ad litem: Shen Zhibeng, lawyer from Beijing No. 9 Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Sun Hai, lawyer from Beijing No. 4 Law Firm.

Defendant: Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette.

Legal representative: Zhu Shixin, Editor-in-Chief of Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette.

Agents ad litem: Zheng Chuanben, Cao Haiyan, lawyers from Shanghai No. 2 Law Firm.

Defendant: Zhao Weichang, male, 29 years old, journalist of Shanghai "League Life".

Agents ad litem: Bao Peilun, Chen Mintao, lawyers from Shanghai Hengxin Law Firm.

The plaintiff, Xu Liang, filed an action with the Jing'an District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendants, Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette and Zhao Weichang, for infringement of reputation rights.

The plaintiff alleged: On December 18, 1987, the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette published an article written by Zhao Weichang titled "The Shock Caused by a 3,000-Yuan Demand" (hereinafter referred to as "The Demand"). Although it did not name me, it obviously referred to me, because among the heroic models of Laoshan, I was the only one who participated in the Shanghai Golden Autumn Art Evening performance. The facts in "The Demand" were seriously inaccurate. Many newspapers and periodicals reprinted and commented on it, and a large number of readers believed it to be true, which seriously damaged my reputation and caused me great pressure and pain in my work and spirit. I request that the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette and Zhao Weichang immediately cease the infringement, publicly publish a clarification in the newspaper to set the record straight, eliminate the impact, restore my reputation, and offer an apology. As for the mental harm caused by the infringement of my reputation rights, I do not request compensation from the two defendants. However, the expenses incurred in litigation for transportation, accommodation, hiring lawyers, etc., totaling RMB 3,700, should be compensated.

The defendant Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette argued: The Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette published "The Demand" under the premise of conducting a perspective analysis of cultural phenomena in society. The facts of the article should be the responsibility of the author. Even if the report in "The Demand" contained inaccuracies, it was a work error. "Inaccuracy" and "infringement" have no direct causal relationship, so it does not constitute infringement of Xu Liang's reputation rights.

The defendant Zhao Weichang argued: The content of "The Demand" was heard at a youth issues seminar, and it was a truthful record of different opinions. The author does not need to investigate and verify the facts of such "news." Because the author had no subjective fault, it does not constitute infringement of Xu Liang's reputation rights.

The Jing'an District People's Court found through public trial: In late October 1987, the office of Shanghai Youth News organized the "Shanghai Youth Golden Autumn Art Evening" and invited the plaintiff, Xu Liang, to perform. As the art evening was of a for-profit nature, when personnel were sent to negotiate performance matters with Xu Liang, they indicated that the actor could be given certain compensation. Xu Liang said that any amount was fine and they could decide. At that time, both parties did not expressly agree on the amount of performance compensation. After Xu Liang performed, the office of Shanghai Youth News decided on its own to give Xu Liang performance compensation. Shortly thereafter, Zhao Weichang, a journalist of Shanghai "League Life," heard statements at a youth issues seminar organized by a relevant unit concerning Xu Liang's demands for payment for his performance in Shanghai, and wrote the article "The Demand," submitting it to the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette. When editing the article, the newspaper anticipated that its publication would harm Xu Liang's reputation, but it did not investigate or verify the facts with the relevant units. It only deleted Xu Liang's name from the article title, changed "demanding" to "price demand," and changed "Xu Liang" in the text to "heroic model of Laoshan," and published it publicly on December 18, 1987, in the newspaper's "Cultural Perspective" column. The article stated: "When a news organization invited a heroic model of Laoshan, who had won the respect and love of the masses with his touching singing, to participate in the Shanghai Golden Autumn Art Evening, this heroic model demanded 3,000 yuan, not one cent less. Despite repeated explanations by the newspaper colleagues that compensation would be given as appropriate based on various factors such as funding, he never changed his tune." After the article was published, many newspapers and periodicals reprinted it and published commentary articles, causing the article to be widely circulated. As a result, Xu Liang was criticized from many quarters. For this reason, Xu Liang entrusted lawyers to negotiate with the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette, but to no avail.

The Jing'an District People's Court held: Citizens enjoy the right to reputation in accordance with law, and the dignity of citizens' persons is protected by state law. The defendant Zhao Weichang, without investigating or verifying baseless rumors, wrote an article and submitted it to the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette. When editing the article, the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette anticipated that publication of "The Demand" would harm Xu Liang's reputation, but without verifying the facts, and after concealing the plaintiff's name, it published the article, thereby expanding the adverse impact in society. Pursuant to Article 101 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the above actions of the two defendants infringed upon the plaintiff's right to reputation. The defendants' denial of their infringing acts is groundless. Pursuant to Paragraph 1 of Article 120 of the General Principles of the Civil Law, the plaintiff's demands for cessation of infringement, elimination of impact, restoration of reputation, and compensation for direct economic losses caused by the litigation are reasonable and should be supported. Based on the facts of infringement by the two defendants, Zhao Weichang shall bear certain responsibility, and the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette shall bear primary responsibility. As for the mental harm caused, the plaintiff does not request compensation, and that is permissible.

Accordingly, on June 10, 1988, the Jing'an District People's Court ruled:

1.  The defendants, Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette and Zhao Weichang, shall cease infringement of Xu Liang's reputation rights, and within ten days after the judgment takes effect, publish a statement in a municipal daily newspaper of Shanghai to restore Xu Liang's reputation and eliminate the impact. The content of the publication shall be subject to court review, with the Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette bearing 70% of the costs and Zhao Weichang bearing 30%.

2.  The Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette shall compensate Xu Liang for economic losses totaling RMB 2,590; Zhao Weichang shall compensate Xu Liang for economic losses totaling RMB 1,110.

The defendants Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette and Zhao Weichang, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed separately to the Shanghai Intermediate People's Court on the same grounds as their defenses at first instance.

The Shanghai Intermediate People's Court held after trial: When the appellant Zhao Weichang wrote the article "The Demand," he failed to investigate or verify the rumor that the appellee "demanded 3,000 yuan" and "not one cent less," resulting in the article's content being seriously inaccurate. Subjectively, he was at fault; objectively, he slandered and disparaged Xu Liang's personal dignity, causing adverse consequences, and thus constituted infringement of Xu Liang's reputation rights. The appellant Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette, knowing that publishing "The Demand" would harm Xu Liang's reputation, failed to examine and verify it, and published this seriously inaccurate article, which disparaged Xu Liang's personal dignity, subjected him to widespread criticism, and directly served to amplify the adverse consequences. Its actions were not merely a work error but were also subjectively at fault. According to the spirit of Reply No. 11 (1988) of the Supreme People's Court (Civil Division), which states that newspapers and periodicals are responsible for examining and verifying manuscripts to be published, and if publication infringes upon a citizen's reputation rights, both the author and the newspaper are liable, the grounds of appeal of the two appellants cannot stand. The reasonable and necessary expenses incurred by the two appellants as a result of Xu Liang's lawsuit for infringement of his reputation rights shall be compensated in an appropriate amount according to the standards prescribed by the state. The amounts determined by the original trial were too high; the portion exceeding the standard should not be included in the scope of compensation. Pursuant to Paragraph 1, Subparagraph 2, of Article 151 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), the judgment is as follows:

1.  Affirm Item 1 of the judgment of the original trial court; modify Item 2.

2.  The appellant Shanghai Culture and Art Gazette shall compensate the appellee Xu Liang for economic losses totaling RMB 1,820; the appellant Zhao Weichang shall compensate RMB 780.
